text.content:
The Sabbat is hardly a unified entity - its history, cosmopolitan makeup and penchant for personal freedom guarantee that it is home to numerous splinter groups, or political factions, who have united under the sect's banner to achieve their own ends or to direct the greater body of the sect. It is not unusual to find members of these factions among the packs, though by no means does every Sabbat support a faction - most simply support the Sword of Caine itself.

A character's political faction (or lack of one) is considered just as important to her identity within the Sabbat as her Nature - it defines where she stands on the sect's central tension between loyalty and order on one end and personal freedom on the other, and it shapes who trusts her, who recruits her and who marks her as an enemy. Players are encouraged to choose (or deliberately decline) a faction at character creation as a core part of defining their Sabbat identity.

The major factions described here are the Black Hand and the Sabbat Inquisition (both effectively sects-within-the-sect with their own membership requirements), the Loyalists, and a handful of "lesser factions" - the Status Quo, the Moderates (and their darker offshoot, the Pander Movement), the Ultra-Conservatives, the Old World Tzimisce (and the Order of St. Blaise and Children of the Dracon associated with them), and the Infernalists, who are not truly a faction so much as a sickness the sect tolerates only by hunting it down.

Stance: Loyalty (militant, sect-first)

The Black Hand - also called the Hand or, less formally, the manus nigrum - is best described as a sect within a sect: a unique militia of vampires distinct from, yet entirely loyal to, the rest of the Sabbat. It draws most of its membership from the Assamite and Gangrel antitribu and from militant vampires of any clan for whom clan loyalty is a tertiary concern next to the Sabbat's ideal of freedom.

Conceived as a specialized militia, the Black Hand is a military force at the disposal of Sabbat leaders, specializing in everything from intrigue and intelligence-gathering to assassination to outright physical combat. The Hand seldom remains fully active for long; instead it dispatches small, focused units or packs as needed. Sabbat elders prefer this arrangement, fearing that a fully active Hand kept too long at the ready might attempt a coup - though throughout its history the Black Hand has served with unwavering loyalty, and is credited with holding the sect together through two Sabbat civil wars.

Members of the Black Hand bear a permanent, mystical sigil branded into the palm of the right hand. Once marked, a vampire is a true member of the Hand and must heed its call whenever summoned; the brand may be concealed (useful for Hand spies) but never removed. Membership lasts until Final Death.

What It Means for a Character

Black Hand membership marks a character as both an elite warrior and an outsider to normal pack politics - clan matters less to her than the Hand's call. She is broadly trusted by archbishops and cardinals for her discipline, but also quietly feared as a potential instrument of a coup. Statute 13 of the Code of Milan obliges all Sabbat to support the Black Hand, so even Sabbat who distrust the Hand are bound to aid its members. Sabbat are expressly forbidden from holding membership in both the Black Hand and the Sabbat Inquisition simultaneously, and rumors of rivalry/antagonism between the two factions are common.

Stance: Loyalty (zealous, doctrinal)

Taking its cue from the mortal Spanish Inquisition, the Sabbat Inquisition is a political faction charged with rooting out heretics and infernalists - and it resembles its mortal namesake in other ways too: an accusation of infernalism from the Inquisition is unlikely to be successfully denied, and the faction is not shy about torturous interrogation tactics. Because it holds the power to depose bishops, archbishops, pack priests and ducti, the Inquisition is also a political entity in its own right, though it has so far avoided becoming a mere political tool, largely because its members are genuinely devout in their duties and respond poorly to attempts at manipulation.

The Inquisition has recently doubled in size, from 15 to 30 members, owing to its successes. All members are respected, trusted and powerful Sabbat. Cells of Inquisitors travel to Sabbat-held territories presiding over trials and delivering punishment, usually in nomadic groups of five accompanied by a pair of templars. Despite its successes, the Inquisition has made few friends - many bishops and archbishops resent the disruption and prying scrutiny that follows wherever Inquisitors travel.

What It Means for a Character

A member of the Inquisition carries genuine authority - even over bishops and archbishops - and is expected to pursue heresy and infernalism with zealous, occasionally brutal rigor. She is treated with deference tinged with dread by local Sabbat leadership, since her presence means scrutiny of everyone's secrets. Like the Black Hand, Inquisition membership is exclusive of Black Hand membership by sect rule, and a quiet, simmering rivalry exists between the two factions.

Stance: Freedom (individualist, anti-authority)

The Loyalist faction claims to be the legacy of the "true" Sabbat - the vampires who shook off the yoke of their elders and seized their own freedom. Other Sabbat tend to dismiss Loyalists as anarchists, sociopaths and spoiled childer who want the benefits of the Curse of Caine without any of the responsibilities.

The Loyalists' philosophy is simple: each vampire is her own master, free to do as she wills, whether that means working to destroy the Antediluvians or going on a rampage through a suburban mall. In practice, few Loyalists indulge in such recklessness, knowing it invites unwanted attention from mortal authorities and other vampires who value secrecy. Loyalists contend that the night no longer belongs to the Sabbat as a body - sect is irrelevant given the modern apathy and infighting of elders, and Sabbat packs are as powerless as Camarilla neonates or rabid anarchs as a result. Loyalists accept anyone into their ranks and maintain no codes or secret rituals to identify one another.

What It Means for a Character

A Loyalist resists hierarchy and answers chiefly to her own conscience and her pack, not to bishops or archbishops. She is suspected (often fairly) of being unreliable when orders conflict with her personal agenda, and other Sabbat may write her off as an anarchist sympathizer. Because Loyalists have no formal organization, rites or insignia, claiming the label costs nothing mechanically to assert - but it costs trust with anyone who values the sect's hierarchy.

Stance: Centrist, lesser faction

As their name suggests, things are good enough for the Status Quo. Made up primarily of Lasombra, Tzimisce and key members of the Black Hand, the Status Quo accepts the nature of vampires and believes that meaningful change is essentially impossible. The Great Jyhad continues regardless, and shaking the foundations of the Sabbat only distracts the sect from its greater goals. The Status Quo does not seek to increase the sect's authoritarianism - hoarding power for its own members would only provoke rebellion in the lower ranks - but it also has little patience for the increasingly vociferous demands of Loyalists and Moderates, and supports compromise that keeps the sect functioning as-is.

What It Means for a Character

A Status Quo member is a pragmatic institutionalist: not a zealous authoritarian, but deeply skeptical of reform movements and the upheaval they invite. She is generally trusted by established leadership precisely because she isn't pushing for change, and she tends to broker compromises between more extreme factions rather than picking fights.

Stance: Center-Freedom, lesser faction

The Moderates oppose what they see as increasing rigidity intruding into the sect. Edicts such as the Purchase Pact and the revised Code of Milan limit the rights of individual Sabbat for the supposed good of the few. While not as vehement as the Loyalists, Moderates nonetheless oppose the encroachment of "rules and guidelines" that they feel have no place among creatures like vampires. The faction rests between Loyalist dogma and Status Quo conservatism, acknowledging the need for some order and structure but not blind adherence to arbitrary codes that offer no benefit to offset their inconvenience. Moderates generally oppose sieges and crusades (though they usually follow orders when given), and they do not hesitate to question those in charge if an order seems foolish or reckless.

The Pander Movement

The Pander Movement represents what the Moderates could become if they abandoned the pursuit of greater freedom in favor of the naked pursuit of greater power. Not all Panders share this mindset, and many Moderates from other clans tread uncomfortably close to the Panders' philosophy of convenience over ideals without formally joining them. The Panders focus on doing whatever is necessary to gain power and authority within the Sabbat - if that means supporting the Status Quo one week and allying with the Loyalists the next, they will do so without hesitation to save their own skins.

What It Means for a Character

A Moderate questions authority without rejecting it outright, and is trusted to follow orders even while voicing dissent. A character aligned with the Pander Movement specifically is viewed with more suspicion - a useful ally in the moment, but one whose loyalty is understood to be for sale to whichever faction currently holds the advantage.

Stance: Loyalty (authoritarian), lesser faction

Predictably composed of the eldest members of the Sabbat - most belonging to Clans Lasombra and Tzimisce - the Ultra-Conservatives favor centralization and authoritarianism, hoping to turn the Sabbat into a disciplined military force against the Antediluvians and the Camarilla. The time for freedom is over, the Ultra-Conservatives claim; Gehenna looms, and it is time to stabilize the sect before it fails utterly. Ultra-Conservatives favor strong leaders and the Ritus of Monomacy, ritually removing weak leaders through duels. The Black Hand seems to be slowly leaning toward supporting the Ultra-Conservatives, though it remains characteristically quiet on the issue.

What It Means for a Character

An Ultra-Conservative character believes deeply in hierarchy, strength and discipline, and openly disdains the Sabbat's culture of personal freedom as a liability in the face of Gehenna. She finds natural allies among elders and the Black Hand, but is viewed by Loyalists and Moderates as a dangerous reactionary who would gladly trade the sect's founding ideals for survival.

Stance: Isolationist, lesser faction

Not every Tzimisce supports the Sabbat wholeheartedly - and among the arcane Tzimisce of the Old World, few support it at all. Openly opposing the Sabbat invites destruction at the hands of self-important packs eager to strike at elders "for the good of the sect," so most Old World Tzimisce find it easier to nominally join the society while abstaining from its meetings, keeping to themselves and maintaining castles on ancestral lands like the voivodes of old.

The Order of St. Blaise

Founded on the medieval veneration of St. Blaise (one of 14 saints associated with healing throat maladies, whose feast involves a blessing of the throat), the Order of St. Blaise leads dangerous unlives by integrating its members into the hierarchy of the Roman Catholic Church. Through careful manipulation of Church resources and visible "good works" at the community level - establishing herds in soup kitchens, exempting buildings from tax status - the Order expands Sabbat influence locally in ways most Sabbat traditionally neglect. Sabbat cities touched by the Order often see a rise in Church attendance as desperate mortals seek any salvation available in the World of Darkness.

What It Means for a Character

An Old World Tzimisce character is reclusive and resistant to sect entanglement, more loyal to ancestral land and lineage than to Sabbat doctrine; she is rarely seen at councils and is trusted only as far as her self-interest aligns with the sect's. A character in the Order of St. Blaise, by contrast, is deeply embedded in mortal institutions and uses subtlety, charity and infiltration rather than force to grow Sabbat power - an unusual profile for a Sabbat vampire that other sect members may view with confusion or distrust.

Stance: Contrarian, lesser faction

A bizarre knightly order of Tzimisce vampires, the Children of the Dracon seem to bear more Hellenic features than the Slavic heritage of Clan Tzimisce would suggest. They appear to be a cultural division, almost a bloodline, though the distinction is more artificial than a true deviation in the vitae. Their exact agenda is unknown, but they seem to be at intellectual odds with the rest of the Tzimisce, consistently playing devil's advocate: if the Tzimisce favor a siege, the Children argue for restraint; if the Fiends support the Inquisition, the Children argue against giving any faction too much power. The Children appear to see themselves as warders of their clan-kin - perhaps atoning for, or guarding against repetition of, some ancient decision that affected the entirety of the Tzimisce clan, possibly even the origin of the clan's weakness.

What It Means for a Character

A Child of the Dracon habitually argues the minority position and resists letting any single faction accumulate too much unchecked power, even when doing so makes her unpopular. Other Tzimisce regard her with a mix of irritation and grudging respect; she is rarely a power player herself, but is often a deciding voice when factions are evenly split.

Stance: Not a true faction - a sickness within the sect

Infernalists - devil-worshippers, Satanists, followers of the Path of Evil Revelations - are not truly a faction within the Sabbat. Rather, they are a sickness that plagues it. Infernalists have no formal structure, as they rarely associate with one another; the business of trafficking with demons is a solitary, medieval practice, and the infernalist is typically a lone conjurer dealing with devils for her own forbidden knowledge. Infernalism runs contrary to everything the Sabbat believes in - while most infernalists see themselves as taking a shortcut to power, they are in truth selling themselves into demonic servitude, which the Sabbat considers wholly antithetical to the sect's sworn ideal of freedom. Hunting infernalists is the Sabbat Inquisition's leading purpose, and woe to the infernalist whose demonic patron deserts her as her foes close in.

See also: the Path of Evil Revelations (packs/paths-of-enlightenment), the alternate Path of Enlightenment that many infernalists follow in place of Humanity.

What It Means for a Character

A character revealed as an infernalist is not merely an unpopular faction member - she is a marked target for the Inquisition and a pariah to virtually the entire sect. Infernalism is not a faction a player declares proudly at chargen; it is the kind of dark secret an antagonist or a tragically compromised character might carry.
